judgments.title: ASHAR BIN SABTUAWAN v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: Criminal Appeal – Appeal against conviction and sentence – Offences under Section 14(a) and Section 15(a)(i) of the Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017 – Victim is a child - Victim alleged the accused fondled her breast in a storeroom of a “surau” and appeared nude in front of her - Victim a person with a disability (OKU) under the category of persons with a learning disability – Victim lodged a police report and her statement was recorded during the CIC – No eye-witness to the incident - Accused denied the incident took place – Not possible because during the incident a community (“gotong-royong”) activity was ongoing at the “surau” – Evolvement of the law on competency of a child witness and acting on uncorroborated evidence of a child – Victim a competent witness - Whether the evidence of the victim is credible for the conviction of the accused to be safe – Learned Sessions Judge found the victim’s evidence consistent and her credibility was not challenged – Whether the Learned Sessions Judge erred in her assessment of the victim’s evidence - Whether the victim’s narration of the incident to the other Prosecution witnesses and her CIC statement recorded are corroborative evidence - Victim gave contradictory evidence about whether the physical sexual assault and the non-physical sexual assault on her actually took place – Victim did not answer and remained silent when the Prosecutor asked her to explain her contradictory answers during re-examination – It was the previous Learned Sessions Judge who observed the victim’s demeanour - Whether the question of corroboration arise when the victim’s evidence itself is not credible in the first place – The applicable law in relation to relying on uncorroborated evidence of a child witness – Whether amendments to the law of evidence are generally characterized as procedural in nature – Whether statutes dealing with the admissibility of evidence have retrospective effect – Whether based on the victim’s CIC statement, the Investigating Officer failed to investigate a boy who purportedly witnessed the incident from the window of the storeroom – Whether an adverse inference ought to be drawn against the Prosecution – Whether the evidence of the victim on the existence of this boy is unclear - Whether the Prosecution had proven both the charges against the accused beyond a reasonable doubt - Whether the conviction is safe.

judgments.title: AWP PROPERTIES SDN. BHD. v CARLSON CONSTRUCTION SDN. BHD.
judgments.catchwords: This case concerns a construction contract dispute between the Plaintiff and the Defendant involving claims for liquidated and ascertained damages (LAD), completion and rectification costs, and outstanding progress payments. The main legal issue was whether the Plaintiff's agreement to allow the Defendant until 31.1.2022 to complete the works constituted an extension of time, thereby disentitling the Plaintiff from claiming LAD for the earlier period of delay. judgments.catchwords: * CRIMINAL LAW: Dangerous Drugs – Trafficking – 81.77 grams of Methamphetamine – Section 39B(1)(a) Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 – Joint charge – Common intention – Section 34 Penal Code – Drugs found concealed inside a jacket in the basket of a motorcycle parked inside an unfenced, shabby residential compound – Elements of possession, custody, control, and knowledge – Distinction between general possession/control of a vehicle and conscious possession of concealed items inside it at the material time – Chan Pean Leon, PP v Denish Madhavan, and PP v Badrulsham Baharom applied. * CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Close of prosecution's case – Prima facie case – Section 180(4) Criminal Procedure Code – Duty of trial Judge to subject prosecution evidence to maximum evaluation – Availability of two or more reasonable inferences – Duty to adopt inference most favourable to the accused – Looi Kow Chai, Balachandran, and PP v Mohd Radzi Abu Bakar applied. * EVIDENCE: Possession – Access by third parties – Duty of prosecution to exclude possibility of access by others – Information-based raid following brief five-minute observation from 200 metres away – Unfenced compound, loosely latched zinc door, and large openings in walls allowing external entry – Nearby car wash and eatery lacking toilets – Failure to guard motorcycle area during raid – Whether prosecution discharged burden of excluding third-party access – PP v Ong Cheng Heong, Ibrahim Mohamad, and Chan Wei Loon applied. * EVIDENCE: Statutory presumptions – Section 37(d) and Section 37(g) Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 – Presumption of knowledge of concealment under s 37(g) against occupier of premises – Whether s 37(g) dispenses with prosecution's burden to independently prove physical custody and control – Prohibition against double presumptions (Muhammed Hassan v PP) – PP v Muhamad Nasir Shaharuddin applied. * CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Investigation – Duty of Investigating Officer to conduct fair, thorough, and impartial investigation – Failure to record statements from three independent civilian witnesses arrested at nearby car wash who witnessed the raid – Inconclusive mixed DNA profile from at least three individuals on jacket wrapping drugs – Negative fingerprint results – Cumulative effect of investigative lapses raising reasonable doubt – Tan Chun Cheng v PP and Magendran Mohan v PP applied. * EVIDENCE: Chain of evidence and contemporaneous records – Delay of over five hours in preparing Search List (P11) and seven hours in lodging police report (P10) – Clerical date error on exhibit markings – Omission of pill count in search and handover forms – Effect on overall evaluation of prosecution's case. * CRIMINAL LAW: Common intention – Section 34 Penal Code – Joint charge against husband and wife occupying same house – Absence of evidence of pre-arranged plan, agreement, or overt act having nexus to the offence – Mere spousal relationship and joint occupation insufficient to infer common intention – Farose Tamure Mohamad Khan and Leow Nghee Lim applied. * EVIDENCE: Burden of proof and cross-examination – Prosecution's erroneous reliance on ss 101–103 Evidence Act 1950 to shift burden onto defence to call third-party witnesses at prosecution stage – Distinction between denied defence suggestions and suggestions admitted or answered with "saya tak tahu" by prosecution witnesses – AH Hosseinzadeh Bashir v PP distinguished.

judgments.title: AMINUL ISLAM BIN ABDUL NOR v CHIN BOON LONG
judgments.catchwords: Catchwords: This is an appeal on my ruling dated 9 September 2026 to transfer the Plaintiff’s suit from the High Court to the Session’s Court following this Court’s motion under Order 57 rule 1A of the Rules of Court 2012 – the transfer was carried out pursuant to the Court’s exercise of its discretion suo motu under Order 57 rule 1A of ROC 2012 – there were 8 Impugned Defamatory Statements – this is a case of defamation where Defendant have published statements which are allegedly defamatory to the Plaintiff – the merits or otherwise of both party’s claims and counterclaims have not been adjudicated in Court – it must be emphasized that before a Court can transfer the proceedings to Session Court on its own motion under O57 r1A ROC 2012 satisfied that doing so is just an appropriate – this determination should be made in the interest of the parties involved while taking into accounts both the subject matter and overall value of the claim – damages including (i) General damages for defamation in the sum of RM100,000,000.00; (ii) Aggravated damages (iii) Exemplary damages – the general damages were quantified which is against Order 18 rule 12 1A of the ROC 2012 – as set out above, the quantum of the claims for reliefs sought by the Plaintiff exceeded RM1,000,000.00 – given that the dispute involves alleged defamation, the Court can take judicial note that, should liability be established, the quantum of damages typically awarded in such cases would not exceed RM1,000,000.00 – this is an appeal on my ruling and not my decision nor judgment as defined under section 3 of the Courts of Judicature Act – it is trite the High Court is bound by the principle of stare decisis, the damages to be awarded, if parties succeed, will not exceed RM1,000,000.00 – even though the Court possesses the requisite jurisdiction to hear the proceedings, the issue is whether it is more suitable to transfer the proceedings to the Session Court – After all, a Session Court is vested with jurisdiction when the amount in dispute or value of the subject matter does not exceed RM1,000,000.00 as prescribed by Section 65 of the Subordinate Courts Act – it is evident that an experienced counsel in a defamation suit would anticipate that should they succeed, the damages awarded by the Court are unlikely to exceed the jurisdictional limit of the Sessions Court – it is in the interest of the parties to proceed there for time efficiency and cost-effectiveness – furthermore, the parties’ interest will not be prejudiced as they retain the right of appeal to the High Court – I ordered the present suit to be transferred to the Sessions Court with no order as to costs.
